Why AI fluency, why now

AI is already in your sector. Is your team ready for it?

Computer vision counts fruit and measures leaves. Sensors and models predict yield, disease and milk output. Language tools draft reports, grant bids and supplier emails in seconds. Yet most teams were never taught what AI actually is, where it works and where it fails — which leads to two costly mistakes: ignoring tools that could save hours every week, or buying solutions that never fit the farm, the lab or the data.

AI literacy for agrifood is the ability to understand, use and critically evaluate AI tools in farming, agronomy, food manufacturing and supply chains, and to use them responsibly. It sits between AI awareness (knowing what AI is and its risks) and AI fluency (confidently applying AI to solve new problems).

Training topics

What your team can learn

Each topic works as a stand-alone lecture, a workshop or a module in a longer course. Mix and match them into your own programme.

01

AI fluency foundations: AI literacy for every employee

What AI is and isn't, and how machine learning, computer vision and large language models work, in plain language. Myths, limits and risks, and how to judge AI claims from vendors and the media.

02

AI in agriculture

How AI is used on real farms today: crop monitoring, yield prediction, disease and pest detection, precision spraying, livestock and dairy monitoring, and decision support tools. What works, what is still hype, and how to start a pilot.

03

AI in agrifood

AI across the food chain: forecasting demand, quality inspection, traceability, food safety, waste reduction, packing and logistics, and sustainability reporting.

04

AI in plant phenotyping

Image-based measurement of plants: leaf area, growth, and stress and disease scoring. Cameras, calibration, and detection and segmentation models explained, with real examples from research and commercial growing.

05

Data collection basics for the future of AI

AI is only as good as its data. How to collect, label, store and share field, lab and farm data so it is ready for AI: images, sensor readings, records, metadata and data quality. Best taken before any AI project starts.

06

Basics of robotics and AI in agriculture

How agricultural robots see, decide and act: harvesting, weeding, milking and autonomous vehicles. Sensors, navigation, safety and costs, and what robotics means for farm labour and skills.

07

Generative AI and prompting at work

Hands-on use of AI assistants for everyday tasks: reports, emails, grant applications, technical summaries, research reviews and training materials. Prompt engineering basics, with examples from agriculture.

08

Responsible AI: data, privacy and trust

Who owns farm data, the basics of GDPR, bias and transparency, and writing an AI use policy for your organisation.

09

AI strategy for leaders

A briefing for executives and boards: where AI creates value in your business, how to assess vendors and pilots, what skills your teams need, and how to measure the return.

The law

Support your EU AI Act AI-literacy duty

Article 4 of the EU AI Act requires organisations that provide or use AI systems to take measures to support their staff's AI literacy. It has applied since 2 February 2025. An amendment in force since 27 July 2026 kept the duty, but no longer requires any particular level of AI literacy to be reached.

The Act does not name a course, and the European Commission's guidance says there is no need for a certificate: an internal record of training is enough. Training is one measure an organisation can take; on its own, it does not make an organisation compliant. National market surveillance authorities supervise Article 4 from 2 August 2026.

Sources: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act, Articles 2 and 4; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI, in force from 27 July 2026; European Commission, AI literacy: questions and answers, updated 27 July 2026. This is a summary, not legal advice. Last reviewed 17 October 2026.

Questions, Answered

Frequently asked questions

Do participants need technical or coding skills?

No. Most sessions are designed for non-technical staff. Advanced, hands-on tracks are available for data, R&D and engineering teams.

Can training be delivered online?

Yes. Sessions run live online, in person at your site, or as a hybrid. Recordings can be provided on request.

How many people can attend?

From small teams of 5 to audiences of several hundred. Workshops work best with up to 25 participants per group.

Can you adapt the content to our business?

Yes. Every course uses examples from your sector, whether that is arable, horticulture, dairy, food processing, retail or research. Custom programmes are built around your own goals and data.

Do you offer training in other languages?

Training is delivered in English.

How much does it cost?

Pricing depends on the format, the length, the size of the group and how much is customised. Send a request through the contact form for a tailored quote, usually within two working days.

Can this support funded projects or skills budgets?

AI literacy training can often be included in innovation projects, staff development plans and skills programmes. Get in touch to discuss your situation.

Do participants get a certificate?

On request, each participant can receive a certificate of attendance for a session, which records that they took part. It is a different document from the certificate of completion that the free AI awareness course issues: that one is earned by watching the course and passing its quizzes, and anyone can check it on aiinagriculture.org's verification page.

Is the training accredited?

No. The training is not accredited and does not carry CPD or BASIS points. CPD recognition is being explored, and this page will say so only once it is confirmed in writing.

What is the difference between AI awareness, AI literacy and AI fluency?

AI awareness means knowing what AI is, what it can and cannot do, and where its risks lie. AI literacy means using and evaluating AI tools responsibly in your own work. AI fluency means confidently applying AI to new problems and to the way work gets done.

Does the EU AI Act apply to UK agrifood companies?

It can. The Act applies to providers that place AI systems on the EU market wherever they are based, and to providers and deployers outside the EU whose AI systems produce output used in the EU. Whether that includes your business depends on where your AI systems and their output are used, so take legal advice for your own situation.

Does the EU AI Act require a certificate of AI literacy training?

No. Article 4 asks organisations to take measures to support their staff's AI literacy, and the European Commission's guidance says no certificate is needed: an internal record of training is enough. A certificate of completion can be part of that record, but it does not show that an organisation is compliant.

Is the AI awareness course really free?

Yes: all 15 video lessons, the quizzes and the certificate of completion, for every person on your team. The course site's terms commit to never moving anything offered free behind a payment later.
